title: Dual Latent Memory for Visual Multi-agent System
claim: Prior systems pass information passively as lossy text between agents; ours stores separate latent memories and injects them on demand.
layout: 2 panels split by dashed line, left prior, right ours, color-coded flows
description: A dashed vertical line splits the figure. The left gray panel, 'Textual Transmission', shows Agent Turn N-1 passing information to Agent Turn N through a passive-receive icon. An inset below merges perception (image icon) and thinking (brain icon) into one natural-language document, which feeds the next agent. The larger right panel, 'Dual Latent Memory (Ours)', has a yellow 'Memory Synthesis' zone and a green 'Memory Orchestration' zone, with a teal overlap in the middle. Blue arrows carry visual inputs through perception into a perception memory network icon. Red arrows carry earlier agent turns through thinking into a thinking memory icon. Labeled 'Updating', 'Injection' and 'Triggering' arrows connect both memories to Agent Turn N. The eye goes first to the colorful right panel and its robot icons.
caption: Comparison with existing text-based information transmission, and our proposed dual latent memory tailored for VMAS.
abstract: While Visual Multi-Agent Systems (VMAS) promise to enhance comprehensive abilities through inter-agent collaboration, empirical evidence reveals a counter-intuitive "scaling wall": increasing agent turns often degrades performance while exponentially inflating token costs. We attribute this failure to the information bottleneck inherent in text-centric communication, where converting perceptual and thinking trajectories into discrete natural language inevitably induces semantic loss. To this end, we propose \textbf{L}$\mathbf{^{2}}$\textbf{-VMAS}, a novel model-agnostic framework that enables inter-agent collaboration with dual latent memories. Furthermore, we decouple the perception and thinking while dynamically synthesizing dual latent memories. Additionally, we introduce an entropy-driven proactive triggering that replaces passive information transmission with efficient, on-demand memory access. Extensive experiments among backbones, sizes, and multi-agent structures demonstrate that our method effectively breaks the "scaling wall" with superb scalability, improving average accuracy by 2.7-5.4% while reducing token usage by 21.3-44.8%.
